Massive Antarctic Iceberg A-81 Reaches South Georgia After Years at Sea

30 Oct 2026, 03:19 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Science Desk · Source: science.nasa.gov

Journey of a Massive Berg

Iceberg A-81, a sprawling mass measuring approximately 1,550 square kilometers (600 square miles), has completed a lengthy journey from the Antarctic coastline to the waters surrounding the remote island of South Georgia. After separating from the Brunt Ice Shelf in January 2023, the berg spent more than three years navigating the Weddell Sea before drifting north into the Scotia Sea and approaching the South Atlantic island in late October 2026.

Satellite observations captured the berg's progress as it slowed noticeably upon reaching South Georgia. According to experts monitoring the region, the massive block of ice appeared to be bumping along the edge of the island's underwater shelf. South Georgia has a history of halting large icebergs; notably, Iceberg A-23A ran aground on the same shelf in 2025 before eventually breaking apart.

Background and Formation

While A-81 traveled relatively quickly once it cleared the Weddell Sea, its formation was decades in the making. A major rift in the Brunt Ice Shelf, known as Chasm 1, remained relatively stable for about 35 years before beginning to widen around 2012. Rapid propagation followed by 2019, though the floating ice held on until its final release in early 2023.

Calving events are a natural part of an ice shelf's life cycle. However, the Brunt Ice Shelf has drawn heightened scientific attention due to a series of recent major breakaways near the British Antarctic Survey's Halley Research Station. Alongside A-81, the shelf previously calved Iceberg A-74 in 2021 and Iceberg A-83 in 2024. While A-74 has since disintegrated, A-83 remains intact and is currently trailing A-81 northward alongside other remnants clearing out of the Weddell Sea.

Practical Implications and Verification

Readers interested in the ongoing tracking of polar ice can review satellite imagery and mission updates directly through official scientific archives.

  • What is confirmed: Iceberg A-81 measures roughly 1,550 square kilometers, broke from the Brunt Ice Shelf in January 2023, and reached the vicinity of South Georgia by October 2026, where its movement slowed against the underwater shelf.
  • What remains unknown: The exact timeline of how long A-81 will linger near South Georgia or whether it will follow A-23A's pattern of grounding and eventual breakup cannot be predicted with certainty.
  • How to verify: Original satellite data and imagery reports are published by the [NASA Earth Observatory](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/a-81-reaches-south-georgia/). Additional tracking details are maintained by organizations such as the U.S. National Ice Center.
